newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: FEATURE - Fleeing war, refugees find only hardship in Kabul.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Fleeing war, refugees find only hardship in Kabul.

text.p: Assadullah, his wife and their three children spend their nights huddled together against the chill of the Afghan winter in one corner of a crumbling Kabul school.
Their days aren't much easier. Desperate for money, Assadullah, 35, spent most of one recent day looking for friends or relatives who live in the bombed-out capital, hoping to borrow money for food.
They are among an estimated 80,000 people who have fled south to Kabul since the beginning of the year from the frontlines of Afghanistan's civil war.
Although now a safe distance from the bombs and bullets, the refugees face the new dangers of hunger and repression in a war-shattered city.
Assadullah's family last week fled their home near the town of Charikar, about 60 km north in Kabul, after forces of the purist Islamic Taleban militia retook the area on January 16.

The Taleban, having captured Kabul last September, is now pushing into northern territory held by an alliance between former government military leader Ahmad Shah Masood and northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum.

Assadullah and his family arrived in Kabul on January 22 along a snow-covered road carrying only a copy of the Koran and some rancid bread. He couldn't afford to hire a truck to carry their other possessions.
"All I had were fake 'Dostum' banknotes with me," he said, referring to Afghani notes supplied to the northern alliance from printing plants in Russia and declared worthless by the Taleban.

One of his sons, three-year-old Farid, has caught pneumonia and the children sometimes go an entire day without eating. A mason, Assadullah can't find work in Kabul as the harsh winter has killed off construction activity.
The clean-shaven Assadullah also was beaten by a Taleban patrol for not having a beard, a symbol of piety now mandatory under the strict Islamic laws imposed by the Taleban.
"Look at this bruise," he said, pointing to a contusion on his forehead. "Taleban slapped me and kicked me for shaving while I was looking for a friend to ask for money."

Aid agencies warn that as the numbers of refugees pouring into Kabul rise, so does the risk of famine in the capital, already devastated by a decade of Soviet occupation, seven years of war between rival warlords and now the current fighting.
U.N. officials have estimated that 80 percent of Kabul's population is impoverished.

"We are providing 25 percent of the food requirements of Kabul, to about one quarter of a million people and if this is halted, God knows what will happen," says Ismael Omar of the World Food Programme.

"I once went to a maternity hospital which we assisted with food for patients and a doctor told me, 'You are giving food to the patients but not us.' She said, 'If we are hungry, how can we treat the patients?'" Omar said.

There has been no attempt so far to provide aid specifically to Kabul's refugees, either by aid agencies or Taleban authorities. A fortunate few can turn to friends or relatives living in Kabul but the future looks bleak for most.
